analysis.one_liner: Replaces the entire federal income tax with a flat tax on wages and business income.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the current income tax and replaced it with a single 19% rate (17% after 2004) on wages and business profits above a standard deduction. It would have eliminated the estate tax, the alternative minimum tax, and virtually every tax credit — including the Earned Income Tax Credit. Income from investments — capital gains, dividends, and interest — would not have been taxed at all under the individual side, and it would have locked the flat tax in by requiring a 60% vote of Congress to raise any tax rate.
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest winners are wealthy households, whose income comes largely from capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances — none of which would be taxed under this bill, while the estate and gift tax disappears entirely. High earners gain from one low rate, and businesses gain from the corporate rate dropping from as high as 35% to 19% (then 17%). Employers that sponsor retirement plans gain from the repeal of nondiscrimination rules, contribution limits, and the excise tax on reclaiming excess pension assets.

how_it_helps.text: All individual income tax would be one rate: 19%, dropping to 17% after 2004, applied only to wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above a standard deduction ($25,580 for a married couple, plus $5,510 per dependent) [S2] [S3].
Capital gains, dividends, and interest would not count as taxable income, and the estate and gift taxes would be repealed for deaths and gifts after 2002 [S2] [S3].
The corporate income tax would be replaced with a 19% (then 17%) tax on business income of any business, after deducting wages and business inputs [S2] [S3].
The bill repeals pension nondiscrimination rules, contribution limits, the penalty on early withdrawals, and the excise tax on employers taking back excess pension assets [S2] [S3].
It would eliminate the alternative minimum tax and nearly all tax credits, simplifying filing for households that itemize today [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Working households that currently pay little or nothing because of the Earned Income Tax Credit and other credits would lose those benefits. Homeowners would lose the mortgage interest deduction, and taxpayers would lose deductions for charitable giving and state and local taxes. Because investment income and inheritances go untaxed while wages are taxed, the tax burden would shift toward people who live on paychecks. Government agencies and tax-exempt employers would owe a new 19% tax on the value of noncash benefits like health coverage they provide employees [S3].

drawbacks.text: Repealing all tax credits eliminates the Earned Income Tax Credit, which currently lifts millions of low-wage working families out of poverty or reduces their taxes [S2] [S3].

The bill taxes wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation but not capital gains, dividends, interest, or estates — a design that independent analysts have long noted shifts the tax burden away from wealth and onto paychecks [S2] [S3].
Homeowners lose the mortgage interest deduction and donors lose the charitable deduction, raising effective costs for middle-income itemizers [S2] [S3].

Allowing employers to reclaim excess pension assets without the excise tax, and dropping minimum-participation and nondiscrimination rules for retirement plans, removes protections designed to keep plans from favoring executives over rank-and-file workers [S3].
A large untaxed category of income means a significant revenue loss that either grows deficits or must be made up elsewhere [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Simplification is a real benefit — a postcard-sized return with one rate would spare millions of households the cost and complexity of itemizing. But the distributional cost is heavy: by taxing only wages while leaving investment income and inheritances untaxed, and by wiping out credits for low-income working families, the bill would shift the overall tax burden toward people paid by the hour. The pension provisions also remove safeguards against plans that favor top executives. On balance, the gains flow disproportionately to the wealthiest households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the Tax Simplification Act of 2003 on May 12, 2003 [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, where it stayed [S5].
It drew 3 cosponsors — 2 Republicans and 1 Democrat — and no further action; the last recorded action was a star print ordered on May 19, 2003 [S4] [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the 108th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing graduated income tax, with its credits for low-income working families and its taxation of investment income and estates, remained in place. Supporters of the flat tax gained nothing beyond the introduction of the proposal itself.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but small — 2 Republicans and 1 Democrat joined the Republican sponsor — and because the bill never came to a vote, no roll-call record shows how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: Under the bill, capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances would be untaxed while wages are taxed at a flat rate, and the estate and gift tax disappears. The gains flow to households whose income comes from wealth rather than paychecks, whose interest runs against wage earners' share of the burden.

The top corporate rate of 35% would fall to 19%, then 17%, with a broad base. Lower business taxes can benefit consumers and workers, but the cut is paired with untaxed investment income at the individual level, tilting the overall system toward capital.

Repealing nondiscrimination, coverage, and contribution-limit rules, and allowing employers to reclaim excess pension assets without the excise tax, frees plan sponsors from rules designed to protect rank-and-file workers' benefits.
These employers would owe a new 19% tax on the value of noncash benefits, such as health coverage, they provide to employees — a cost likely passed on through reduced benefits or budgets.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A single-rate tax with a standard deduction and no credits or itemized deductions would sharply reduce demand for professional tax preparation.
